- Model consistently overestimates prices, especially in the early part of the forecast horizon (first 5–10 days).
- Forecasts tend to peak too early and overshoot, then gradually decline — suggesting a lag in recognizing downward momentum.
- After a spike in price (e.g., 72+), model often overreacts with a sharp upward correction, then undercorrects.
- Mean reversion is not adequately captured — model holds too much upward bias, especially when true prices show clear downward drift.
- Forecasts are overly sensitive to recent high values, leading to “herd” behavior — model follows recent peaks rather than adjusting for underlying fundamentals.
- Model underestimates the rate of decline in later days, especially after 20–25 days, where true prices show a steeper drop than forecasted.
- Avoid extrapolating recent trends without checking for structural breaks or policy changes (e.g., auction rules, cap adjustments).
- When true prices drop below 65, model often fails to adjust downward quickly — suggesting a lag in recognizing low-price regimes.
- Forecasts should be capped at 10–15% above recent 7-day average to prevent runaway overestimation.
- Use a moving average of the last 10 days as a baseline to anchor forecasts, especially when true prices show strong mean reversion.
